hints: Focus on what reactivity with oxygen tells you, an element that needs strong heating must be fairly unreactive.
Sort the four elements into metals that make ionic chlorides and non-metals or metalloids that make covalent chlorides.
Look for the one element that fits both clues at once, low reactivity toward oxygen plus a molecular chloride.
walkthrough:
**Use the oxygen clue to judge reactivity**

Think like this, very reactive elements catch fire easily in oxygen with little heating. An element that needs strong heating must be much less reactive.

Reactivity trend: $\text{Na} > \text{Mg} > \text{P} > \text{Si}$ in terms of ease of oxidation

**Use the chloride clue to judge bonding type**

Remember the simple rule, metals lose electrons to chlorine to give ionic chlorides, while non-metals share electrons to give covalent chlorides.

$$\text{Mg} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 \text{ (ionic) }$$
$$\text{Si} + 2\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{SiCl}_4 \text{ (covalent) }$$

**Test each element against both clues**

Sodium and magnesium give ionic chlorides like $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$, so they fail the second clue. Phosphorus gives covalent chlorides like $\text{PCl}_3$, but white phosphorus burns spontaneously in air, so it fails the first clue.

Only silicon needs strong heating to form $\text{SiO}_2$ and forms covalent $\text{SiCl}_4$, so it fits both.

options.A: Magnesium forms an ionic chloride, $\text{MgCl}_2$, not a covalent one. It also burns very readily in oxygen with a bright white flame once ignited, so it does not match the low reactivity description.
options.B: Phosphorus does form covalent chlorides such as $\text{PCl}_3$ and $\text{PCl}_5$, but it is too reactive toward oxygen. White phosphorus ignites in air and red phosphorus burns easily, so it does not require strong heating.
options.C: Sodium is a very reactive Group 1 metal that reacts rapidly with oxygen and forms the ionic chloride $\text{NaCl}$. It fails on both clues, it is too reactive and its chloride is ionic.
options.D: Silicon is a metalloid with a giant covalent structure, so it is quite unreactive and needs strong heating to react with oxygen to give $\text{SiO}_2$. With chlorine it forms $\text{SiCl}_4$, which is a simple covalent molecule. It fits both statements perfectly.
